name: Zane Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Zane. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We've no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office at Hartley's, a family-owned builders' merchant on the edge of town that sells timber, bricks and plumbing gear to tradesmen. I take orders over the phone and at the counter, plan the delivery runs for our two lorries, chase builders who pay late and keep the account books filed in the back room. Most of our customers have been coming for twenty years, so half my job is knowing who's good for credit and who isn't.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the regulars, the builders who come in at seven with a coffee and a list on a scrap of cardboard. What wears me out is the new ordering website the owner's son put in, because half the customers still ring me anyway. I don't use any AI things, never have; I don't trust what I can't check with my own eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because most of it was talk from people who've never done a day's real work. I'd say that at the counter and at church on Sunday. I don't post online, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd suit me fine. My job's steady, Mr Hartley values loyalty, and I've got a good bit put by. I'd carry on as I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as now. Grace and I are getting married next summer, so I'd keep saving for that and a deposit. I might take on a few more delivery-planning duties as Mr Hartley's son pushes his website.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, settled. A builders' merchant runs on trust and a handshake at the counter, and no clever software changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the owner's son and his website. Is that a source of tension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Young Mr Hartley wants everything online and I'm the one who has to answer the phone when it doesn't work. We get along, but we see things differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else on your mind in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Housebuilding slows down when interest rates go up, and then we're quiet. Two winters ago we cut hours for a month. But there are plenty of merchant counters in the area, so I've never felt unsafe.

I'd say it at the **counter and at church**, not online.
think: My job's **steady**, and the owner values loyalty.
With **good savings** put by, I'd carry on as I am.
do: Keep running the **merchant office** exactly as now.
Keep saving for the **wedding and a deposit** with his fiancée.
Take on extra **delivery planning** as the owner's son pushes online orders.
feel: **Calm and settled**, confident in a trade built on trust.
S0.quote: A builders' merchant runs on trust and a handshake at the counter, and no clever software changes that.
fieldNote: Zane trusts what he can check with his **own eyes**, not software.
His real background worry is **building slowdowns** when rates rise.
There's quiet friction with the **owner's son** over going online.

steps.text: Keep running the counter and delivery runs at Hartley's
Keep saving for the wedding and a house deposit with Grace

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have a right to modernise, but they should look after loyal staff. I'd say that to Mr Hartley straight. I wouldn't go running to the government about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is where I'd get caught out. Ordering, booking deliveries, chasing payments, that's what the card lists and it's my day. Young Mr Hartley would jump at it, and I'd be the one who refused to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on whatever training they gave, grudgingly, because I'd rather keep my job than my pride. I'd ask Mr Hartley if I could work more on the yard side, loading and checking deliveries. And Grace and I would put the wedding budget down a bit and save the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A bit angry, too, though I couldn't tell you exactly at whom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather keep your job than your pride. Is that easy for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it isn't. I've told the old man at Hartley's for five years that computers can't be trusted, and now I'd have to go and ask the computer for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Grace say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace works at the primary school, in the kitchen, so her job's safe in this one. She'd say we trust God and we work hard, and we'll be fine. She's usually right.

say: I'd say firms may **modernise** but should look after **loyal staff**.
I'd tell the owner straight, not **run to government**.
think: The card's tasks are **my day**: ordering, deliveries and chasing payments.
I'd be the one who **refused to learn** it, which could cost me.
do: Attend the **training** grudgingly, putting the job before pride.

Trim the **wedding budget** and save the difference.
feel: **Anxious** and somewhat angry, without a clear target.
S1.quote: I've told the old man at Hartley's for five years that computers can't be trusted, and now I'd have to go and ask the computer for help.
fieldNote: Zane's **pride** is the real obstacle, and he names it himself.
He looks to the **hands-on yard** as a safer place.
His **faith and fiancée** steady him more than any policy.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hartley for more shifts loading and checking on the yard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let something like that loose without thinking, and the big tech companies should answer for it. But I wouldn't want the government taking over everyone's lives either. I'd say that at church and to the lads at the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office job's gone within a year. What's left is the yard, and robots come for that three years later. My best bet is my dad, who's a plumber and has always wanted me in the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a plumbing apprenticeship with Dad straight away, even at apprentice wages. We'd still get married, but a small wedding at church with a meal after, and keep most of the savings. I'd stop any spending that isn't needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, I'd say. And a bit ashamed that I didn't listen to Dad years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Plumbing is hands-on, but robots come in 2031. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, but I've seen old houses. A robot that can find the leak behind a 1930s bathroom wall is a long way off, whatever the date on your card says. I might be wrong, but that's what I'd bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your savings are strong. Would you use them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only to get through the apprenticeship. Apprentice pay is half what I get now. The savings would fill the gap for a couple of years, and that's what they're for.

say: I'd say **big tech companies** should answer for letting it loose.
I wouldn't want **government taking over** lives either.
think: The **office job** goes within a year, and the yard three years later.
My best bet is my **dad's plumbing** business.
do: Start a **plumbing apprenticeship** with his father straight away.
Have a **small church wedding** and keep most savings.
feel: **Alarmed**, and a bit ashamed he didn't listen to his father sooner.
S2.quote: A robot that can find the leak behind a 1930s bathroom wall is a long way off, whatever the date on your card says.
fieldNote: Zane expects to **lose his job** within a year.
His **family trade** is the safety net he reaches for, not government.
He bets that **old houses** will defeat robots for a while.

steps.text: Start a plumbing apprenticeship in his father's van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families and businesses to prepare, and people should get on with it rather than waiting for help. I'd say it to the younger lads at the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough to do a proper apprenticeship with Dad. My office job ends, but I'd be qualified by the time it does. That's a fair deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job at Hartley's for a year or two and do the plumbing course at the college on evenings. Then I'd go into Dad's van full-time. Grace and I would have the proper wedding and buy a small house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel I'd got a plan. It's like seeing the weather turn and having time to get the washing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep the office job for a while. Why not start the apprenticeship straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the pay's better at Hartley's and we've got a wedding to pay for. Dad says the evening course is fine for the first part. Five years means I can finish my plumbing course before Hartley's office needs a computer more than it needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Hartley?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight that I'm learning a trade, in case. He's a fair man. He'd probably say good lad.

I'd tell the **younger lads** at the counter to get on with it.

fieldNote: Zane's **self-reliance** shows in preparing through family, not policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and there's no excuse not to be ready. I'd say that to anyone who asked. I'd be a bit more relaxed in how I said it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd take my time, learn plumbing with Dad and take the business over from him one day. I'd be 40 when the robots come, and I don't think they'll be in old houses by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hartley's for a few years, enjoy married life and start the plumbing course in year two or three. I'd keep saving. I'd also tell my younger cousins to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. With ten years to go, I'd take over my dad's plumbing van and never look at a screen again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI now. Would you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd learn plumbing instead. That's my answer to all of it, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would change your mind about plumbing being safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw a robot fix a boiler at a neighbour's house, maybe. I'd believe it when I saw it. Until then I'd trust a spanner.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be in my dad's van on apprentice pay with a new wife and no time to plan. What would help is apprenticeships being easier to start, with businesses getting help to take people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about family. My dad told me to learn a trade when I was sixteen, and the whole AI business has made my dad right.

headlineQuote: My dad told me to learn a trade when I was sixteen, and the whole AI business has made my dad right.
portrait: Zane is a 27-year-old **builders' merchant administrator** who knows every regular's credit.
He **never uses AI** and trusts only what he can check himself.
His **traditional** outlook leans on faith, family and work over government help.
His answer to every serious picture is a **plumbing apprenticeship** with his father.
His wedding to Grace shapes how **fast** he can move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with apprentice pay, a new marriage and no planning time.
whatWouldHelp: Easier **apprenticeships**, with support for businesses to take people on.
